english_translation: Traditional healing methods used roots and tree bark.

dialogue.shona: Nzira dzekurapa dzechinyakare dzaishandisa midzi nemakwati emiti.
dialogue.english: Traditional healing methods used roots and tree bark.
dialogue.literal_gloss: Nzira [nzira] • dzekurapa [dzekurapa] • dzechinyakare [dzechinyakare] • dzaishandisa [dzaishandisa] • midzi [midzi] • nemakwati [and / with makwati] • emiti [emiti]

grammar_notes.title: Joining Words with 'ne-' ('and / with') in 'nemakwati'
grammar_notes.content: Look closely at 'nemakwati'. In Shona, the word for 'and' or 'with' between nouns is not a separate word—instead, the prefix 'ne-' (or 'na-' before people's names) is written attached directly to the second noun! For example, 'ne-' + 'makwati' forms 'nemakwati'. You will see this everywhere in daily speech: 'sadza nemuriwo' ('sadza and vegetables'), 'nesimba' ('with strength'), and 'nekukasira' ('with haste / quickly').
grammar_notes.rule: ne- + Noun = and / with [Noun] (written as a single word, e.g., sadza nemuriwo = sadza and vegetables)

grammar_notes.title: Talking About How Things Used to Be: The '-ai-' Past Habitual ('dzaishandisa')
grammar_notes.content: In this sentence, 'dzaishandisa' uses the past habitual/imperfect marker '-ai-'. Whenever you talk about how people used to live in historical times, or an ongoing state in the past ('used to do', 'was/were doing'), Shona combines the subject prefix with '-ai-' + the verb stem: for example, 'vaigara' ('they used to live'), 'vaitengeserana' ('they used to trade with one another'), 'yaivakwa' ('it used to be built'), and 'hwaizivikanwa' ('it was renowned/known').
grammar_notes.rule: Subject Prefix + -ai- + Verb Stem = 'used to [verb] / was [verb]-ing' (va- + -ai- + -bva = vaibva, 'they came from')

grammar_notes.title: Infinitive Verbs & Action Nouns with 'ku-' ('dzekurapa')
grammar_notes.content: Look at 'dzekurapa' in this sentence. Every Shona verb in its dictionary ('to do') form begins with 'ku-': for example, 'kudya' (to eat), 'kutenga' (to buy), 'kubhadhara' (to pay), 'kuona' (to see), and 'kurwa' (to fight). Because 'ku-' verbs also behave as action nouns ('eating', 'paying', 'working'), you can attach linking prefixes directly to them: 'yekubhadhara' ('for paying'), 'pakubikwa' ('in the cooking'), and 'nekuona' ('by/with seeing').
grammar_notes.rule: ku- + Verb Stem = 'to [verb] / [verb]-ing' (ku- + -tenga = kutenga, 'to buy'; ye- + kubhadhara = yekubhadhara, 'for paying')

cultural_notes.title: Indigenous Herbal Medicine: Healing with Roots ('Midzi') & Bark ('Makwati')
cultural_notes.content: Zimbabwe's indigenous woodlands contain hundreds of medicinal plants whose roots ('midzi'), leaves ('mashizha'), and tree bark ('makwati emiti')—such as the fever tree ('mubvamaropa') and sausage tree ('mumvee')—have been studied by both traditional herbalists and modern pharmacologists.
